e.t: This verb means “to be subject to bleeding” or simply “to bleed.” It describes an ongoing physical loss of blood rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Matthew 9:20. The word itself identifies the condition being experienced; the surrounding verse explains the individual situation in which it appears. Its plain sense therefore concerns someone suffering from persistent bleeding.

“Uncircumcision” refers to the condition of not being circumcised. It can identify a person or group marked by the absence of this physical sign, and it is also used when discussing Jews and Gentiles in relation to circumcision. This Greek New Testament word occurs 20 times in 17 verses, with especially frequent use in Romans. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding context.

This word means “blameless”: free from a charge of wrongdoing or a valid reason for accusation. It describes a person whose conduct cannot rightly be faulted. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Peter 3:14. The word expresses an upright condition that should characterize believers as they await what God has promised. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is clear: living in a way that gives no legitimate basis for blame.

This word means “inexpressible”—something so profound or overwhelming that ordinary words cannot fully communicate it. It describes what cannot be adequately spoken or put into language, rather than merely something difficult to explain. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Peter 1:8. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage, but the central idea remains something beyond complete verbal expression.

e.t: This word means “to pay back” or “to repay.” It describes giving back what is owed or returning something received, and it functions as an action word. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at Philemon 1:19. That single occurrence establishes the word’s basic sense clearly, while the surrounding verse determines the particular situation in which repayment is mentioned.

This Greek New Testament word describes a person who is unforgiving and unwilling to be reconciled. It points to a settled refusal to release a grievance or restore peace with another person. The word appears once in the Greek New Testament, in 2 Timothy 3:3, but the word itself gives this basic description rather than explaining every detail of that verse. Its central idea is a relationship marked by refusal to forgive or make peace.

Ahaz is a personal name referring to a specific man named in Matthew’s genealogy. It is not presented here as a general description, action, or quality, but as the name by which this ancestor is identified. In the Greek New Testament, the name occurs twice, both within Matthew 1:9. Because no verse text or surrounding passage is included here, the name’s broader historical significance should be understood from the genealogy and related Old Testament passages rather than from the name alone.

This Greek New Testament word describes something burdensome or weighty—something carrying substantial heaviness or imposing a serious load. Its meaning can apply to a burden, matter, or quality that is difficult because of its weight or seriousness. The word occurs six times in the Greek New Testament, across Matthew, Acts, 2 Corinthians, and 1 John. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on a literal burden, a serious matter, or weighty speech.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to sail slowly.” It describes the movement of a ship when progress by sea is unhurried or difficult. The word appears once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 27:7. Its basic sense focuses on slow sailing rather than on a particular cause, such as wind, weather, or navigation; those details would require the surrounding verse and passage. As a verb, it expresses what the ship or sailors were doing: moving gradually by sea.

This word means “calm,” describing a state in which disturbance or agitation has ceased. It is a noun, referring to calmness or stillness rather than naming an action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, each in one of the accounts describing Jesus’ command over a storm. The word’s basic sense remains focused on the resulting calm, while the surrounding verse supplies the fuller significance of that event. Its three occurrences are Matthew 8:26, Mark 4:39, and Luke 8:24.

This word describes someone who is afraid or timid—lacking courage in the face of danger or difficulty. It is used in the Greek New Testament as a description of people, rather than as the name of an event or object. The word occurs three times in the New Testament, appearing in Matthew, Mark, and Revelation. Its exact force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains fearful or hesitant behavior.

This word means “builder,” referring to someone who constructs or establishes a structure. It identifies the one responsible for making a lasting work rather than merely using or occupying it. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Hebrews 11:10. The surrounding verse determines exactly how the word’s picture of a builder applies there, but its basic meaning remains a person who builds.

This word is a first-person pronoun, referring to the speaker or to a group that includes the speaker. Depending on its place in a sentence, it can mean “I,” “me,” “my,” “mine,” “we,” “us,” or “our.” It may identify the speaker as acting, receiving something, belonging to something, or sharing in an action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 2,582 times, so its precise English rendering depends on the surrounding sentence.

e.t: “Elamite” refers to a person from Elam, an ancient region. It is a people-designation rather than a description of an action, quality, or belief. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs once, in Acts 2:9, identifying people by their regional origin. The word’s basic meaning is therefore an Elamite: someone belonging to or coming from Elam. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the name itself carries this straightforward geographic meaning.

e.t: This word means “then,” marking what happens next in a sequence of events or statements. It is an adverb that connects one action, person, or development with what follows afterward. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 16 times, showing a recurring role in moving the account or argument forward. Its basic force is temporal and orderly: one thing occurs, and then another follows. The precise nuance in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the word itself points readers to the next step or subsequent event.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to look at” or “to look upon.” It describes directing one’s sight toward someone or something, with the exact force determined by the surrounding sentence. The word occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, in two passages in Luke and one in James. Its basic sense is visual attention: someone looks toward another person or object. It does not by itself establish whether the look expresses admiration, concern, judgment, or simple notice; those meanings must come from the context of each verse.

e.t: This word means “to attempt”—to make an effort toward doing something. It describes the act of undertaking an action, whether or not the effort succeeds. In the Greek New Testament, it appears three times, in Luke and Acts, so its basic sense is consistent across those occurrences. The surrounding verse determines what action is being attempted, but the word itself emphasizes the effort or initiative to begin doing it.

This Greek New Testament word means “to impress” or “to make a good impression.” It describes seeking to affect how others view someone or something, especially by creating a favorable appearance. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Galatians 6:12. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is the deliberate attempt to gain approval or present oneself favorably to others.

Caiaphas is a personal name referring to a particular man in the Greek New Testament. It is not a word describing an action, quality, or object; it identifies the person named Caiaphas. The name appears nine times in nine New Testament verses, from Matthew through Acts, and is rendered consistently as “Caiaphas.” Its precise significance in any individual verse comes from the surrounding passage, but the name itself functions simply as a personal designation.

This word means “theft”—the wrongful taking of what belongs to someone else. It names the act itself rather than a person who steals or an object that is taken. In the Greek New Testament, it appears twice: once in Matthew 15:19 and once in Mark 7:21. Its basic sense remains focused on stealing or unlawfully taking property, while the surrounding verse determines how the word functions in each passage.

This word means “cumin,” a small aromatic spice used in cooking. The related spelling “cummin” reflects the same plant or seasoning. In the Greek New Testament, the word occurs once, in Matthew 23:23. Its basic meaning identifies the spice itself; the word does not by itself describe a person, action, or spiritual quality. The surrounding verse is needed to explain why cumin is mentioned there.

This word means “insanity,” referring to a state of irrational or disordered thinking. It is a noun that names such a condition rather than describing a person’s character or making a general statement about mental health. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only once, in Acts 26:24. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise force in that passage must be understood from the immediate context, but its central sense remains a severe departure from sound reason.

This Greek New Testament word means “to gnaw,” describing the action of chewing or biting persistently. It functions as an action word, focusing on what someone does rather than naming a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Revelation 16:10. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the repeated act of gnawing. e.t: This word means “to measure”—to determine an amount, extent, or standard. It is a verb describing the act of using a measure or setting a measured standard. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 11 times across 9 verses, including passages in Matthew, Mark, Luke, 2 Corinthians, and Revelation. Its repeated rendering as “measure” supports this central sense. The surrounding verse determines what is being measured, but the word itself describes the measuring action rather than a particular object or result.

This Greek New Testament word means “calf,” referring to a young bovine animal. It is used as a concrete noun for an animal mentioned in several different settings, including Luke, Hebrews, and Revelation. The word occurs six times in six New Testament verses, so its basic meaning remains consistent across those passages. The surrounding verse determines the particular role or significance of the calf in each setting.

e.t: This word means “from where” or “whence,” pointing to the place or source from which someone or something comes. It is used to ask or indicate origin, direction, or source rather than describing the thing itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 15 times across 15 verses, including passages in Matthew, Luke, Acts, Hebrews, and 1 John. Its precise force in a particular sentence depends on what person, place, or source the surrounding words identify.

e.t: This word means “to take” or “to take with.” It describes taking, receiving, or bringing someone or something, and it can especially indicate taking another person along. Its precise sense depends on what is being taken and the surrounding sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 49 times, showing that it is a regularly used word for an act of taking or accompanying rather than a rare or specialized expression.

This word refers to the sea, especially the open sea or broad waters. It identifies a large body of water rather than a small pool, river, or shoreline area. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Matthew and Acts, and both occurrences are rendered “sea.” Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains a sea or open expanse of water.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to enrich” or “to make rich.” It describes the giving or receiving of abundance, whether understood as material provision or as being richly supplied in another way. The word occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, in 1 Corinthians and 2 Corinthians. Its basic sense is increase: someone is made richer, better supplied, or more abundantly provided for. The surrounding verse determines what kind of enrichment is intended in each use.

e.t: This New Testament verb means “to care for” or “to provide for.” It describes taking thought for another person’s needs and making practical provision for them. The word appears three times in the Greek New Testament, in Romans 12:17, 2 Corinthians 8:21, and 1 Timothy 5:8. Its use points to responsible concern expressed through action, rather than mere awareness or feeling. The surrounding verse determines who is being cared for and what provision is required.

This word means a corpse, a dead body rather than a living person. It refers to the physical remains of someone who has died. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs seven times in six verses, including passages that speak of a body being buried, left exposed, or gathered where birds assemble. The wording can be rendered as “corpse,” “corpses,” or “dead body,” with the exact English form shaped by the sentence. Its central idea remains the lifeless body of a dead person.

e.t: This word describes someone who is feverish—literally, someone burning with a fever. It refers to the condition of having a fever rather than to a particular cause, treatment, or outcome. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Matthew 8:14 and Mark 1:30. Its wording functions as a description of a person’s physical condition, while the surrounding verse supplies the specific situation in which that condition appears.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to be dark” or “to darken.” It describes the loss or absence of light, whether something becomes dark or is darkened. The wording can also be rendered “were darkened,” showing that it may describe a change taking place rather than merely name a condition. It occurs five times in the Greek New Testament, in Matthew, Mark, Romans, and Revelation. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

e.t: This word means “to agree with.” It describes reaching or expressing agreement with another person, statement, or matter. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times, showing a repeated idea of people being in agreement or acting with someone’s consent. Its basic sense remains straightforward: to share agreement rather than oppose what has been said or decided. The surrounding verse determines exactly what or whom the agreement concerns.

e.t: “To travel with” describes accompanying someone on a journey or going along beside them. It presents movement shared with another person rather than travel done alone. In the Greek New Testament, this word appears once, at Acts 9:7. Because the verse text is not included here, the surrounding details are not stated; the basic meaning remains the act of accompanying someone while traveling. It functions as a concise description of companions who are journeying together.

This word refers to mental soundness and propriety: a settled, sensible way of thinking that expresses itself in fitting and proper conduct. It points to self-control and sound judgment rather than confusion, excess, or disorder. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, including one rendering as “propriety.” Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a sound mind expressed through appropriate behavior.

This word means “path” or “paths,” referring to routes or roads that people travel. It is a plural noun, so it describes more than one such route when used in this form. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, each time rendered “paths.” Its basic meaning is straightforward: established ways of passage, whether understood as physical routes or as part of a broader statement whose precise force comes from its surrounding context.

Phanuel is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Luke 2:36. The name itself does not provide a broader definition or explain the person’s role; those details must come from the surrounding passage. Its consistent English rendering is “Phanuel,” matching the supplied lexical gloss.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to explain”—to make the meaning of something clear to another person. It describes the act of giving understanding rather than merely mentioning or repeating something. In ordinary Bible usage, it points to making a statement, teaching, or matter understandable. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Matthew 15:15. Its basic sense remains focused on clear explanation.

e.t: This word means “to cool” or “to grow cold.” It describes a change from warmth to coldness and can be used figuratively when something that was active or fervent loses its warmth. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Matthew 24:12. Its basic sense is the diminishing or disappearance of warmth, whether understood literally or as a picture of something becoming less fervent. The surrounding verse determines how that sense is applied there.
